arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical deep-dives on four compiler optimization areas: (1) SSA construction, (2) alias analysis, (3) register allocation, (4) inlining.
arguments.instructions:
For each of the four areas, name and explain at least three specific named real mechanisms/algorithms in depth (not a shallow list). Use precise standard compiler terminology throughout.

Required depth per area:

1. SSA construction: Cover at least three of: the Cytron-Ferrante-Rosen-Wegman-Zadeck (CFRWZ) dominance-frontier algorithm for phi-node placement; dominator tree computation (Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm); the 'braun/buchwald/mehler/mallon/zwinkau' or 'simple and efficient SSA construction' (sreedhar-gao style or Braun et al. 2013 approach using predecessor filling and block sealing); semi-pruned/pruned SSA (live-variable pruning to minimize phi nodes); SSA destruction (translating out of SSA, dealing with the 'lost-copy' and 'swap' problems, Sreedhar-Gao out-of-SSA translation); minimal vs. pruned vs. semi-pruned SSA forms. Explain dominance frontiers precisely, phi-node insertion criteria, and renaming via dominator-tree-based variable versioning.

2. Alias analysis: Cover at least three of: Andersen's inclusion-based points-to analysis (and its cubic complexity); Steensgaard's unification-based points-to analysis (near-linear complexity via union-find); type-based alias analysis (TBAA) as used in LLVM/C strict aliasing; flow-sensitive vs flow-insensitive analysis; context-sensitive vs context-insensitive (k-CFA); field-sensitive vs field-insensitive heap modeling; must-alias vs may-alias; the use of alias sets and memory SSA (MemorySSA in LLVM). Explain the trade-offs in precision vs scalability.

3. Register allocation: Cover at least three of: graph-coloring register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs algorithm, simplify/select/spill worklists, optimistic coloring); Chaitin's original iterated register coalescing variant; George-Appel iterated register coalescing (conservative coalescing, briggs vs george coalescing tests); linear scan register allocation (Poletto-Sarkar) and its use in JIT compilers; SSA-based register allocation (Hack/Grund/Goos, using chordal graph properties of SSA interference graphs); live-range splitting; spill cost estimation; the interference graph construction and node degree/spill heuristics.

4. Inlining: Cover at least three of: bottom-up vs top-down inlining; call-graph based inlining with inline cost models (e.g., LLVM's inline cost analysis, GCC's inline heuristics); profile-guided inlining using PGO/hot-path heuristics; devirtualization-enabled inlining (speculative inlining with guards for virtual calls / polymorphic inline caches); partial inlining; inlining and its interaction with recursion (recursive inlining limits, inlining budgets/thresholds); link-time/whole-program inlining (LTO-based cross-module inlining).

Write dense, precise, well-organized technical prose with correct standard terminology. Target roughly 600-900 words per area. This is a research/writing task, no code execution needed.

arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical deep-dives on four compiler optimization areas: (5) escape analysis, (6) loop vectorization, (7) instruction scheduling, (8) loop optimizations.
arguments.instructions:
For each of the four areas, name and explain at least three specific named real mechanisms/algorithms in depth (not a shallow list). Use precise standard compiler terminology throughout.

Required depth per area:

5. Escape analysis: Cover at least three of: connection-graph-based escape analysis (Choi/Gupta/Midkiff/Moreira style used in JVM HotSpot); scalar replacement of aggregates enabled by escape analysis (stack allocation of non-escaping objects, eliminating heap allocation); thread-escape analysis for synchronization elision (lock elision/biased locking enabled by provably thread-local objects); method-local vs global escape states (NoEscape, ArgEscape, GlobalEscape classification as in HotSpot's EA); partial escape analysis (points where an object escapes only on some control-flow paths, as in Graal's partial escape analysis with deoptimization); the interaction with allocation sinking.

6. Loop vectorization: Cover at least three of: SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization vs loop vectorization; loop-level vectorization with strip-mining and vector-length-based loop trip count remainder handling; dependence analysis for vectorization legality (distance vectors, direction vectors, the Banerjee test, GCD test); vectorization cost models (LLVM's VPlan-based cost model); handling reductions in vectorized loops; gather/scatter for non-contiguous memory access vectorization; loop peeling/unrolling for alignment; predicated/masked vectorization for handling control flow (if-conversion).

7. Instruction scheduling: Cover at least three of: list scheduling (priority-based list scheduling with ready lists); basic-block scheduling vs. global/regional scheduling; trace scheduling (Fisher's trace scheduling for VLIW with compensation code); software pipelining (modulo scheduling, the iterative modulo scheduling algorithm, minimum initiation interval computation via resource and recurrence constraints); the sethi-ullman algorithm for expression tree evaluation order/register minimization; superblock/hyperblock scheduling; critical-path scheduling and its heuristics (e.g., scheduling by priority = critical path length).

8. Loop optimizations (beyond vectorization): Cover at least three of: loop-invariant code motion (LICM) with its dominance/safety conditions; loop unrolling (full vs partial, and interaction with branch prediction); loop fusion and loop fission/distribution (with legality via dependence analysis); loop interchange (for locality, legality conditions via dependence direction vectors); loop tiling/blocking for cache locality; induction variable recognition and strength reduction (linear IV analysis, canonical induction variables); loop unswitching (hoisting invariant conditionals out of loops); loop-closed SSA form (LCSSA) and its role enabling other loop transforms.

Write dense, precise, well-organized technical prose with correct standard terminology. Target roughly 600-900 words per area. This is a research/writing task, no code execution needed.
